```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(AlphaSimR)

```

# Introduction

Most simulations start from founder genomes simulated by `runMacs` or
`quickHaplo`. Sometimes it is better to start from real data: the
haplotypes or genotypes of an existing breeding population, a genetic
map from a linkage study, or marker effects estimated in a genomic
prediction model. This article shows how to bring each of these into
`AlphaSimR` and start a simulation from them.

Three functions create a founder population from external data:

| Function | Input | Use when |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `importHaplo` | phased haplotypes | the phase of every allele is known |
| `importInbredGeno` | genotypes of inbred lines | the individuals are fully inbred, so genotypes give the haplotypes |
| `newMapPop` | lists in `AlphaSimR`'s internal format | another function has produced that format already |

All of them need a genetic map, which `importGenMap` formats. Each
returns a `MapPop`, or a `NamedMapPop` when a pedigree is supplied, that
is passed to `SimParam$new` like any other founder population.

So that the article can run anywhere, its examples make their own
stand-in for external data instead of reading files from disk.

# The genetic map

A genetic map is a `data.frame` whose first three columns are the
marker name, the chromosome and the map position. Here is a small map,
in centimorgans as it would usually come from a linkage study:

```{r genMap}
mapCM = data.frame(
  marker = paste0("snp", 1:8),
  chr = rep(c("1", "2"), each = 4),
  posCM = c(0, 35, 80, 115, 5, 30, 60, 85)
)
mapCM
```

`AlphaSimR` measures map positions in Morgans, so positions in
centimorgans are divided by 100. Positions are absolute, measured from
the start of the chromosome. They are kept as supplied, so they must not
be negative, and a map that starts at 5 cM leaves 5 cM before its first
marker in which crossovers can still occur.

```{r importGenMap}
genMap = data.frame(
  marker = mapCM$marker,
  chr = mapCM$chr,
  pos = mapCM$posCM / 100
)
str(importGenMap(genMap))
```

By default each chromosome ends at its last marker. When the full
length of a chromosome is known, give it with `genLen`, one value per
chromosome in Morgans, so that crossovers beyond the last marker are
simulated too. Each length must be at least the position of the
chromosome's last marker.

```{r genLen}
genLen = c(1.25, 0.95)
```

# Phased haplotypes

`importHaplo` takes a matrix with one row per haplotype and one column
per marker. The haplotypes of an individual are in consecutive rows, so
for a diploid the first two rows are the two haplotypes of the first
individual. Alleles are coded 0 and 1, and the column names are the
marker names used in the genetic map.

Here we stand in for real data by drawing haplotypes for six diploid
individuals at random.

```{r haplo}
nInd = 6
haplo = matrix(rbinom(2 * nInd * nrow(genMap), size = 1, prob = 0.5),
               nrow = 2 * nInd)
colnames(haplo) = genMap$marker
head(haplo, 4)
```

A pedigree is optional. With one, the individuals keep their own IDs
and parents, and the result is a `NamedMapPop`. It can be a vector of
IDs, or a `data.frame` whose first three columns are the ID, mother and
father.

```{r importHaplo}
ped = data.frame(id = paste0("ind", 1:nInd),
                 mother = "0",
                 father = "0")

founderPop = importHaplo(haplo = haplo,
                         genMap = genMap,
                         ploidy = 2L,
                         ped = ped,
                         genLen = genLen)
founderPop
```

The imported haplotypes come back unchanged:

```{r checkHaplo}
all(pullSegSiteHaplo(founderPop) == haplo)
```

For large data sets the haplotype matrix can be stored as `raw`, which
uses one byte per allele instead of eight. `pullSegSiteHaplo`,
`pullSnpHaplo` and `pullMarkerHaplo` return this format with
`asRaw = TRUE`, which makes it easy to keep a subset of a population's
markers, as when a sequence is thinned to the density of a SNP array:

```{r rawHaplo}
keep = genMap[c(1, 3, 5, 7), ]
rawHaplo = pullMarkerHaplo(founderPop, markers = keep$marker,
                           asRaw = TRUE)
thinnedPop = importHaplo(haplo = rawHaplo, genMap = keep)
thinnedPop
```

# Genotypes of inbred lines

Genotyping usually gives unphased genotypes rather than haplotypes. For
fully inbred lines that loses nothing, because both haplotypes are the
same. `importInbredGeno` takes genotypes with one row per individual,
coded either 0, 1, 2 or -1, 0, 1; it detects which. Heterozygous or
fractional values are rounded to the nearest homozygote.

```{r importInbredGeno}
geno = 2 * matrix(rbinom(nInd * nrow(genMap), size = 1, prob = 0.5),
                  nrow = nInd)
colnames(geno) = genMap$marker

inbredPop = importInbredGeno(geno = geno, genMap = genMap,
                             ped = paste0("line", 1:nInd))
pullSegSiteGeno(inbredPop)
```

# PLINK files

PLINK's text format stores a pedigree and genotypes in a `.ped` file
and the map in a `.map` file. The `.ped` file has six columns describing
each individual (family, ID, father, mother, sex and phenotype) followed
by two allele columns per marker. The `.map` file has four columns:
chromosome, marker name, position in centimorgans and position in base
pairs.

Both are plain text and can be read with `read.table`. To make a pair
to read, we write one with `writePlink`, which needs a simulation with a
trait and a SNP chip.

```{r writePlink}
SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
SP$nThreads = 1L
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 2)
SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.5)
SP$addSnpChip(nSnpPerChr = 2)
pop = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)

baseName = file.path(tempdir(), "example")
writePlink(pop, baseName = baseName, simParam = SP)
```

Read the two files back, keeping the alleles as text. `AlphaSimR` has
no physical map, so `writePlink` fills the base pair column with each
site's index on its chromosome.

```{r readPlink}
pedFile = read.table(paste0(baseName, ".ped"), colClasses = "character")
mapFile = read.table(paste0(baseName, ".map"), colClasses = "character")
mapFile
```

`writePlink` codes the alleles as "1" and "2". Each marker's two allele
columns are split into the individual's first and second haplotype,
recoded to 0 and 1, and interleaved so that each individual's two
haplotypes are in consecutive rows. The map positions are converted from
centimorgans to Morgans.

```{r plinkToHaplo}
alleles = as.matrix(pedFile[, -(1:6)])
allele1 = alleles[, seq(1, ncol(alleles), by = 2), drop = FALSE]
allele2 = alleles[, seq(2, ncol(alleles), by = 2), drop = FALSE]

plinkHaplo = matrix(0L, nrow = 2 * nrow(alleles), ncol = ncol(allele1))
plinkHaplo[seq(1, nrow(plinkHaplo), by = 2), ] = (allele1 == "2") * 1L
plinkHaplo[seq(2, nrow(plinkHaplo), by = 2), ] = (allele2 == "2") * 1L
colnames(plinkHaplo) = mapFile$V2

plinkMap = data.frame(marker = mapFile$V2,
                      chr = mapFile$V1,
                      pos = as.numeric(mapFile$V3) / 100)

# PLINK lists the father before the mother
plinkPed = data.frame(id = pedFile$V2,
                      mother = pedFile$V4,
                      father = pedFile$V3)

plinkPop = importHaplo(haplo = plinkHaplo, genMap = plinkMap,
                       ped = plinkPed)
all(pullSegSiteHaplo(plinkPop) == pullSnpHaplo(pop, simParam = SP))
```

This round trip keeps the phase only because `writePlink` writes each
individual's haplotypes in order. Genotypes from a SNP array or from
sequencing are not phased: PLINK does not record which allele of a
heterozygote is on which haplotype. Treating the first allele column as
one haplotype would then pair alleles at random, which breaks up the
linkage disequilibrium in the data. Inbred lines can be imported with
`importInbredGeno`, but outbred individuals, such as most animals,
should be phased with dedicated phasing software before their
haplotypes are imported. Real PLINK files also tend to code alleles as
nucleotides and to mark missing genotypes with "0", so each marker
needs recoding to 0 and 1 against a chosen reference allele, and
missing genotypes need imputing first.

PLINK's binary `.bed` format is not plain text. Packages that read it,
such as `genio` and `BEDMatrix`, return a genotype matrix that can be
handled as above.

# Starting a simulation

An imported founder population starts a simulation in the usual way.
When the causal loci and their effects are known, for example from a
mapping study, `SimParam$importTrait` adds a trait from marker names and
effects instead of sampling them. Here two markers on each chromosome
are given additive effects:

```{r importTrait}
SP = SimParam$new(founderPop)
SP$nThreads = 1L
SP$importTrait(markerNames = c("snp1", "snp3", "snp6", "snp8"),
               addEff = c(0.5, -0.25, 0.4, 0.1),
               name = "Yield")
```

`domEff` adds dominance effects. Additive-by-additive epistasis is added
with `epiPairs`, a two-column matrix naming the interacting pairs of
markers, and `epiEff`, their effects. Every marker must then be in
exactly one pair, and a pair may span two chromosomes.

```{r importTraitEpi}
SP$importTrait(markerNames = c("snp2", "snp4", "snp5", "snp7"),
               addEff = c(0.3, 0.2, -0.1, 0.4),
               epiPairs = rbind(c("snp2", "snp5"),
                                c("snp4", "snp7")),
               epiEff = c(0.2, -0.3),
               name = "Height")
```

A SNP chip whose markers are known, such as a commercial array, is
added by marker name with `addSnpChipByName`:

```{r addSnpChipByName}
SP$addSnpChipByName(markers = c("snp1", "snp2", "snp5", "snp6"),
                    name = "Array")
```

The founders then carry their own IDs into the simulation, and every
function works as usual:

```{r newPop}
pop = newPop(founderPop, simParam = SP)
pop@id
gv(pop)
pullSnpGeno(pop, snpChip = "Array", simParam = SP)
```

# Further reading

The [Demographic Models](DemographicModels.html) article shows how to
import founder genomes simulated by msprime and stdpopsim, and the
[Gene Drop Simulations](GeneDropSimulations.html) article shows how to
simulate genomes through a known pedigree, starting from imported
founders.
